Input: Which ontology term represents the concept I have in mind — for example heart attack — and what is its identifier?
Output: Use OLS to search for your concept, filter by class and relevant ontology, and open the best matching term. Check its definition and synonyms, then copy its identifier. Searching for heart attack in MONDO finds myocardial infarction (MONDO:0005068).

Input: I have an ontology identifier such as MONDO:0005068 in my data — what does it mean?
Output: Paste the identifier into OLS search and open the result from its defining ontology. Read the label, definition, synonyms, cross-references and relations. For example, MONDO:0005068 identifies myocardial infarction, also known as heart attack.

Input: What are the broader and narrower terms of myocardial infarction — its parents, its children and everything beneath it?
Output: Open the term in OLS and inspect the Tree panel for ancestors. Expand the term and its children to explore narrower terms, or use the Graph view for other relationships. For complete lists, use the API's children, hierarchicalDescendants or hierarchicalAncestors endpoints and follow pagination.

Input: Which ontologies cover my subject area, and is a particular ontology suitable — what is its scope, which version is loaded, how big is it and under which licence is it published?
Output: Use OLS's Ontologies page to filter by category, name, identifier or description. Open candidate ontologies and inspect their scope, version, class counts and licence in Ontology Information. Browse their contents or search within each ontology to assess whether it covers your subject area.

Input: Is the term I am using still current? If it has been made obsolete, which term should I use instead?
Output: In OLS, enable Include obsolete terms and search for the identifier. Open its defining ontology's result and check for a deprecated notice. Follow Replaced by or term replaced by when available, and confirm the replacement's definition. Some obsolete terms have no recorded replacement.

Input: Which ontology terms are mentioned in this piece of text — a sample description, an abstract, a protocol?
Output: Use OLS's Tag Text page: paste text or drop a plain text file to highlight matches and list ontology terms. Filter by ontology, adjust minimum match length and substring settings, review the matches, then download selected results as CSV. Matching uses labels and previously curated text.

Input: I can describe what I mean in everyday words — for example ringing in the ears — but I do not know what ontologies call it. Which terms mean the same thing?
Output: Use OLS embedding search: enter your phrase, choose an embedding model under Search Model, and search. Filter by ontology and inspect the highest-ranked terms. Check each candidate's definition because similarity scores do not establish correctness. For an existing term, explore Similar Classes on its page.

Input: How do I look for terms in just one part of an ontology — for example, offer only heart disorders when someone types "infarc" into a form field?
Output: Use the OLS API's select endpoint for autocomplete or search endpoint for full searches. Supply q, ontology and childrenOf with the branch root's IRI URL-encoded once. Read response.docs and store the selected identifier. Use allChildrenOf to include additional hierarchical relationships such as part of.

Input: How can my AI assistant, or an application built on a large language model, look terms up in OLS instead of guessing identifiers?
Output: Connect your assistant to the OLS remote MCP server at https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ols4/api/mcp using Streamable HTTP with no authentication. Confirm its tools are available, then ask it to use OLS to search terms or explore hierarchies. Verify returned identifiers and definitions in OLS.

Input: I have a term in one ontology — for example myocardial infarction, MONDO:0005068. What is it called in other ontologies and coding systems such as MeSH, ICD-10-CM or SNOMED CT?
Output: Use OxO to search by identifier, IRI or label. Select target ontologies if needed, then review the mapped terms, relationship predicates and evidence. Distinguish exact matches from close, broader or narrower matches, and inspect mapping details before accepting inferred equivalences.

Input: I have a list of terms from one ontology. What are their equivalents in a specific target — for example, which ICD-10-CM codes correspond to my Mondo disease terms — and which of my terms have no equivalent there?
Output: Use OxO’s Multiple terms mode: paste or upload identifiers, select the target in To ontologies, and search. Review and download the mappings as SSSOM TSV. Compare downloaded subjects with your inputs to identify unmapped terms, or use the batch-map API’s unmappedInputs list.

Input: Which terms in one ontology correspond to terms in another — for example, all mappings from the Human Disease Ontology (DOID) to the Experimental Factor Ontology (EFO) — and can I have them as a file?
Output: Use OxO with the term box empty. Choose the source in From ontologies and the target in To ontologies, then search. Apply any evidence filters and download the complete mapping collection as SSSOM TSV. Swap the ontologies and search again to examine the reverse direction.

Input: Can I rely on this mapping? Who published it and on what basis — and if OxO inferred it, from which published mappings?
Output: In OxO, open the mapping’s eye icon to inspect Mapping Details. Review justification, confidence, provenance and mapping set. For inferred mappings, inspect the asserted premises and derivation graph under Inference Details; assess reliability from the underlying published mappings and their evidence.

Input: OxO returns many mappings for my term. How do I keep only the ones I am prepared to use — for example only published ones, only exact matches, or only those a curator made by hand?
Output: Use OxO’s column filters: Type for asserted mappings, Predicate for exactMatch, and Mapping justification for ManualMappingCuration. Combine filters as needed, limit Distance, or choose mapping sources under More options. Download the filtered results or save the results-page URL to reproduce your selection.

Input: I searched OxO for a term that I know exists, and got nothing (or less than I expected). Are there really no mappings — or are they hidden?
Output: In OxO, open More options and enable cross-references, subclass links or obsolete terms, then search again. Check ontology direction, try partial label matching or an identifier, and verify the prefix is recognised. Read predicates carefully: a cross-reference or subclass link does not establish equivalence.

Input: Where do OxO's mappings come from? Which mapping sets does it hold, what is in a particular set, and how do I search within just that set?
Output: In OxO, open More options, then Choose specific mapping sets to browse and select sources. Search with those sets selected to restrict results. Click a Mapping set link in the results to inspect its description, provider and contents, filter its mappings, or download them as SSSOM TSV.

Input: A mapping in OxO looks wrong to me. Which source published it — or, if OxO inferred it, which of the published mappings it rests on is wrong — and whom do I tell?
Output: In OxO, open Mapping Details and follow the Mapping Set link to identify the publisher. For an inference, inspect its asserted mappings and identify the faulty premise. Report that assertion to its publisher, including identifiers, predicate, mapping-set ID, details-page link and evidence explaining the error.

Input: A column of my dataset holds diagnoses as people typed them. How do I turn that column into standard ontology terms and into codes of a coding system such as ICD-10-CM — and know which results I can rely on?
Output: Deduplicate the values and map them with Zooma. Check doubtful suggestions and find missing terms in OLS. Translate accepted identifiers into target codes with OxO, starting with asserted mappings and reviewing gaps or alternatives. Record decisions, preserve unresolved values for manual coding, and join results back to your dataset.

Input: My data were annotated with ontology terms some years ago. Which of those terms have since been made obsolete, and what should each be replaced with?
Output: Use OLS to identify obsolete terms and check their stated replacements. Where none is named, search OxO with obsolete terms included; if unresolved, map the original wording with Zooma. Validate every replacement in OLS, then update your data using a dated table of old identifiers, replacements and reasons.

Input: I want to analyse two datasets together. One records diagnoses as free text, the other as codes from several coding systems. How do I bring both to a common set of terms, so that I can match records and group them?
Output: Choose a common ontology in OLS. Map free text with Zooma and codes with OxO, initially limiting mapping distance to one. Review ambiguous results in OLS and use its hierarchy to assign broader groups. Add validated terms and groups to both datasets, retaining original values and codes.

Input: Zooma has suggested a term for my value, but with a confidence below 90% — or it has suggested several. Is the suggestion right, and how do I check?
Output: Use OLS to inspect each doubtful Zooma suggestion's definition, synonyms, hierarchy and obsolete status. Accept suitable terms, replace unsuitable ones using Zooma's alternatives or OLS, and record your decisions outside Zooma because its on-screen feedback is not saved in downloads.

Input: I know the concept in words — say heart attack. What is the ontology term for it, and what are the corresponding codes in other vocabularies, such as ICD-10-CM, MeSH and SNOMED CT?
Output: Search OLS for the concept, choose an appropriate ontology and confirm the term's definition. Copy its identifier into OxO, select the target vocabularies and search. Review mapping predicates and provenance, preferably starting with asserted exact matches, then copy or download the codes.

Input: OxO says two terms are an exact match. Before I merge data on the strength of that, do the two terms really mean the same thing?
Output: Inspect the mapping's predicate, provenance and derivation in OxO. Compare both terms' definitions, synonyms and positions in the OLS hierarchy. Accept equivalent meanings, retain broader or narrower relationships without merging records, or reject incompatible mappings. Check codes absent from OLS at their home resource.

Input: I need every code that belongs to a subject area — for example, to select all records about diabetes. Which terms does an ontology place under diabetes mellitus, and which codes in my coding system (say ICD-10-CM) correspond to them?
Output: Use OLS to identify the top term and list it with its descendants. Batch-map these identifiers in OxO to your coding system, initially keeping asserted mappings. Review unmapped terms and possible broader codes. Expand codes in the coding system itself if you need every subdivision.

Input: My values are free text, but the system I am loading them into wants identifiers from one particular vocabulary — MeSH headings for literature searching, say, or ICD-10-CM codes. How do I get from the text to those identifiers?
Output: Use Zooma to map your text to a suitable bridging ontology, such as Mondo, and review the suggestions. Convert accepted identifiers to prefix:code format, batch-map them in OxO to the target vocabulary, and download asserted mappings. Join both results by term identifier and review unresolved values.

Input: Zooma found nothing for one of my values, or nothing that fits. How do I find the right term myself — and what do I do if there isn't one?
Output: Review Zooma's alternatives first. Then search OLS using your wording, synonyms or an embedding model, and browse a broader term's children. Check candidate definitions and parents. If only a broader term fits, preserve the original text; if none fits, request a term through the ontology's issue tracker.

Input: I have a list of free-text values — sample attributes, column values, questionnaire answers. Which ontology term best matches each of them?
Output: Use Zooma’s Map Strings tab. Paste one value per line, optionally followed by a tab and its type, choose suitable target ontologies, and click Map. Review suggested terms, confidence and provenance, resolve ambiguous matches, and download the suggestions as TSV.

Input: My project annotates with particular ontologies. How do I make Zooma suggest terms from those ontologies only — or prefer them over others?
Output: In Zooma, open Which ontologies to map to? and choose custom ontologies or a preset. Add your ontologies and drag them into preference order. Leave Include results from other ontologies unticked to restrict suggestions, or tick it to allow additional ontologies. Map your values again.

Input: My values are in a column of a spreadsheet, perhaps with a second column saying what kind of thing each value is. How do I get ontology terms for that column without retyping it?
Output: Export your spreadsheet as CSV or TSV, then use Zooma’s Upload CSV. Check the delimiter and header settings, select the Term column and optional Type column, import and map. Download suggestions, select appropriate matches, and join them back using textToMap and propertyType where supplied.

Input: I have a sentence or paragraph — a sample description, a clinical note, part of a methods section. Which parts of it can be annotated with ontology terms, and with which terms?
Output: Use Zooma’s Annotate Text tab. Paste the passage, choose ontologies appropriate to its content, and click Annotate Text. Review highlighted phrases and their suggested terms, remove irrelevant phrases, and download the suggestions as TSV. Map any important missed phrases separately through Map Strings.

Input: Zooma suggested a term for my value. Why that term? If it is not right, what else could it have been — and how do I keep a record of what I decide?
Output: In Zooma, click Prediction Type to inspect Mapping Provenance and use thumbs down to view alternatives. Check term definitions in OLS and choose the appropriate term. Record accepted, replaced or unresolved mappings in your own spreadsheet: on-screen decisions are not saved or reflected in the downloaded TSV.

Input: Has a curator at one of the EMBL-EBI data resources already mapped this text to an ontology term? And how do I control which resources' curated mappings Zooma draws on?
Output: In Zooma, open Where to get mappings? to include or exclude curated data resources and drag them into priority order. Map your values, then inspect Curated entries in Prediction Type and their Source. Review provenance and confirm each curator’s original context fits your intended use.

Input: Where to start if I have a concept in words, and I want its ontology term?
Output: Use OLS to search for your word or phrase. Filter results by ontology and class, then open a suitable term and check its definition and synonyms before copying its identifier.

Input: Where to start if I have a concept in mind, without knowing the correct words, and I want its ontology term?
Output: Use OLS embedding search to describe the concept in everyday words. Choose an embedding model, optionally filter by ontology, and check the definitions of the suggested terms before selecting one.

Input: Where to start if I have an identifier, and I want to know what it means?
Output: Use OLS to search for the identifier. Open the term in its defining ontology and read its label, definition, synonyms, cross-references and relationships to understand what it means.

Input: Where to start if I have an identifier, and I want its equivalent in another vocabulary?
Output: Use OxO to search for the identifier and select the target vocabulary under To ontologies. Review each mapping's relationship, evidence and source before choosing an equivalent identifier.

Input: Where to start if I have many identifiers, and I want their equivalents in another vocabulary
Output: Use OxO's Multiple terms search to paste or upload your identifiers and select the target vocabulary. Review and download the mappings, then identify unmatched inputs by comparing the results with your list or using the batch-map API.

Input: Where to start if I have many free-text values, and I want ontology terms?
Output: Use Zooma to map your free-text values to suggested ontology terms. Review doubtful or competing suggestions in OLS by checking definitions, synonyms, hierarchy and status. Accept or replace each suggestion and record your decisions outside Zooma.

Input: Where to start if I have many free-text values, and I want codes of a coding system?
Output: Use Zooma to map distinct free-text values to ontology terms, OLS to check doubtful suggestions, and OxO to translate accepted terms into the target coding system. Review ambiguous or missing mappings, record decisions, and join the results back to your dataset.

Input: Where to start if I have a passage of text, and I want the terms mentioned in it?
Output: Use Zooma's Annotate Text tab to paste your passage and select suitable ontologies. Run annotation, inspect the highlighted phrases and suggested terms, discard irrelevant phrases, and download the results.

Input: Where to start if I have a mapping I am unsure of, and I want a reason to trust it or not?
Output: Use OxO to inspect the mapping's relationship, provenance and supporting assertions. Compare both terms in OLS using their definitions, synonyms and hierarchy, then decide whether to accept the mapping, treat it as a looser relationship, or reject it.

Input: Where to start if I have a mapping I believe is wrong, and I want to know who published it and where to report it?
Output: Use OxO's mapping details to identify the publishing mapping set. For an inferred mapping, trace the faulty supporting assertion. Follow the source to its publisher or the ontology's issue tracker through OLS, and report the mapping identifiers, evidence and reason for correction.

Input: Where to start if I have old annotations, and I want current ones?
Output: Use OLS to identify obsolete terms and stated replacements. If none is named, try OxO mappings, then Zooma with the original text or old label. Check every proposed replacement in OLS and keep a dated record of identifier changes.

Input: Where to start if I have two datasets annotated differently, and I want one combined dataset?
Output: Choose a common ontology in OLS. Use Zooma to map free-text values and OxO to translate existing codes into that ontology. Check ambiguous results and choose broader groups in OLS, then add the common terms and groups to both datasets before combining them.
